paras: The lynching of Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie took place at Rico, Colorado, at about 2 a.m. on June 16, 1882, when a party entered the town jail, took out the two prisoners and hanged them in a small cabin opposite. The men were accused of killing Rico's marshal, and the wire report of their deaths ran in papers across the country under headings such as "Two Murderers Lynched in Colorado." Only one syndicated brief described them as "two colored desperadoes."

According to a Denver dispatch printed in the Las Vegas Daily Gazette, Trinidad Charley and Thomas Walsh had killed Marshal Smith of Rico about ten days before the lynching. The same dispatch said they were captured on a Sunday and brought to Rico on the following Wednesday. A Durango report of June 15 stated that on their arrival the citizens of Rico "made a strong demonstration" to seize the prisoners, but the force escorting them was too strong. That report added that it was believed they would not live until the next day.

A special to the Denver Republican, dated at Rico on June 16, reported that at 2 o'clock that morning a party entered the jail and took out Wall and Trinidad Charlie. The two men were shackled together by leg and arm, and they were hanged in a small cabin opposite the jail. From the appearance of Charlie's body, the correspondent wrote, it was evident that he had made a strong resistance. The lynchers were not named or counted; the wire called them "a party," the Las Vegas Gazette "vigilantes," and several brief notices "a mob."
No report of an inquest, arrests of the lynchers or any official response appears in the coverage.

The story reached most readers as the Denver wire, which the Evening Star in Washington, the Richmond Daily Dispatch and the Savannah Morning News printed nearly word for word between June 17 and 19. These versions called the dead men "the murderers" and gave no account of the evidence against them. Western papers used lighter headings, the Helena Weekly Herald calling it "Another Necktie Party" and the St. Paul Daily Globe "A Labor of Love." Shorter notices in Sacramento, Missouri and Rhode Island reduced it to a line about two murderers taken from jail by a mob.

A syndicated crime column carried by the Watertown Republican and the Brookings County Sentinel was the only coverage to give a race, saying Wall and "Trinidad Charley," "two colored desperadoes," were "hoisted into eternity" by "Judge Lynch." The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic reprinted the wire beneath an editorial headed "The Yankee Ku Klux," which complained of "lawless lynchings" at the North and West while defending the lynching of Black men in the South.

Accounts differed slightly on the time, with the syndicated brief placing the lynching on "the night of the 15th" and the Omaha Daily Bee at "two o'clock Friday night," while the Rico-dated wire, the closest source, put it at 2 a.m. on June 16. The Las Vegas Gazette spelled the first man's name "Thomas Walsh," and the St. Paul Daily Globe garbled it as "Chas. Noll."

reader.title: Lynching of Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie
bases: A party described as a 'mob' or 'vigilantes' took two prisoners held for murder from the Rico jail at night and hanged them (A3, A8, A7, A25).

Two jailed men accused of killing Marshal Smith were taken out at 2 a.m. by a 'party' that other papers called a 'mob' and 'vigilantes' and hanged without trial (A3, A8, A7, A21); the pretext was punishment for the alleged murder (A1, A8).
The Denver wire (A2, A3), a separate Denver dispatch in the Las Vegas Gazette (A8), and a Durango report of an attempt the day before (A1) agree on the core event; no report denies it.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Denver wire unchanged, calling the men 'the murderers' and the lynchers 'a party', under heads such as 'Two Murderers Lynched in Colorado'.
Western papers used jocular heads: 'Another Necktie Party' (Helena) and 'A Labor of Love' (St. Paul).
The Raleigh Farmer and Mechanic used the wire to charge the North and West with hypocrisy under 'The Yankee Ku Klux', while defending Southern lynchings.
A syndicated brief alone gave race, 'two colored desperadoes', 'hoisted into eternity' by 'Judge Lynch'.

versions.value: 2 a.m. June 16 ('this morning', dispatch dated June 16)

conflicts.note: The night of June 15-16 reconciles most versions; the Rico-dated wire (A3) is the best evidence. The Omaha 'Friday night' would fall a day later and is likely loose wording.
Spelling variants of one man; 'Wall' is in the Rico special.
Only one syndicated brief, printed days later far from Colorado, names a race; it does not contradict the wire but is not confirmed by it.
